concept: Leveraged looping and recursive lending: LST SOL loops and stablecoin loops with carry math

claims.text: A Kamino elevation group (eMode) is a curator-defined cluster of correlated assets (stablecoins, LSTs with their underlying SOL, wrapped assets with natives). A user joins voluntarily; the program then applies the group's LTV and liquidation threshold in place of per-reserve defaults. Leaving the group, or borrowing an asset outside it, restores the per-reserve defaults. (high confidence)

A market supports at most 32 elevation groups (IDs 1-32; 0 means no group). Per the docs, a single reserve can opt into up to 20 groups, and group parameters only apply to reserves that list the group ID in their own elevation_groups array. (medium confidence)

Group configuration is not exposed through the REST API; a curator sets it through the SDK or Kamino CLI. Setting allow_new_loans to 0 pauses new borrows in a group while existing positions keep their relaxed parameters and can still repay and exit. (low confidence)

Kamino's eMode is the elevation group. One lending market stores up to 32 groups (ids 1-32; id 0 means no group). Each group sets ltv_pct, liquidation_threshold_pct, max_liquidation_bonus_bps, allow_new_loans, max_reserves_as_collateral and exactly one debt_reserve. (high confidence)

Y differs in durability by source, and that sets how much of L×Y a planner can rely on. Kamino separates structural yield (staking 'exists whether or not anyone is using Multiply') from fee-driven yield (JLP) and credit-market yield (RWAs), 'both of which can compress or disappear'. Ethena's sUSDe reward is funding and basis income that 'will vary considerably (even day to day)' and can be zero. Chaos Labs shows part of the appeal of sUSDe loops is Ethena points. A loop sized on a funding or incentive yield carries a Y that can fall to zero while B stays positive. (medium confidence)
Kamino Swap is the execution layer for all Multiply flash-loan swaps (open, adjust, close) and uses multi-DEX routing to get the best output. (medium confidence)

Incentive-driven carry can disappear without a price move. Curvance's example shows a loop moving from positive to negative carry when a temporary token-reward campaign ends, so Y should be split into organic yield and rewards. (low confidence)

Kamino prices LSTs (JitoSOL, mSOL, bSOL) by stake rate (SOL_staked / LST_minted) read from the on-chain stake pool account, not by DEX price, so a temporary market depeg neither changes position health nor triggers liquidation. The same design exposes positions to genuine backing impairment such as a staking-protocol exploit, which lowers the stake rate. (high confidence)

The SDK's default Multiply open builder orders the transaction: refresh oracles; create or wrap token accounts; flash-borrow the collateral token from the collateral reserve; deposit; request the elevation group between deposit and borrow; refresh reserves and obligation; borrow the debt token; swap debt to collateral; flash-repay. A second builder flash-borrows the debt token first (swap, then deposit and borrow, then repay). Kamino's docs give a simplified seven-step order with the swap before the deposit. Because the default flash loan comes from the collateral reserve, it needs unborrowed collateral-token liquidity there. (medium confidence)

Leverage as an equity multiplier (C*Pc / (C*Pc - D*Pd)) measures balance-sheet amplification, not net price exposure. If collateral and debt are the same asset or highly correlated, net delta can be small even when measured leverage is high (IFCA). Kamino makes the point for SOL liquid staking loops: both legs are SOL-denominated, so LTV does not move with SOL's USD price; what moves it is the LST/SOL exchange rate and the gap between staking yield and the SOL borrow rate. (medium confidence)

In the mSOL episode the lending venues' oracle choice decided who was liquidated. Marginfi priced assets at market, using a one-hour exponential moving average per Solana Compass, and said its liquidations fairly reflected market operations. Solend priced mSOL off the SOL oracle and said it does not treat an LST depeg as a liquidation trigger. SolanaFloor is a Jito Network subsidiary, and Solana Compass labels its write-up AI-generated, so treat these details as secondary. (medium confidence)

A debt-side stablecoin depeg matters only if the venue marks it. Jupiter Lend values dollar-stablecoin debt (USDC, USDT, USDG, USDS, JupUSD, PYUSD) at exactly $1 with no price feed, so a stablecoin depeg neither triggers nor prevents liquidation there (EURC debt uses a EUR/USD feed). Kamino instead applies price bands that reject stablecoin prices outside an expected range. Collateral-side stablecoin depegs and rate inversion remain risks for stable loops. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

In the Kamino SDK flow, slippagePct also sizes the flash loan so that the worst-case swap fill still covers the repayment. The swap quote's priceAInB must be the mid price (before slippage). Passing a minimum-out price counts slippage twice and sizes the position wrong. Slippage also absorbs the gap between the best quoted route and the route actually sent. (medium confidence)

Solana transaction size limits constrain which swap route a deleverage can use. Kamino's examples compress each KSwap route candidate with address lookup tables and send the first candidate that fits, sorted by best output. The best-output route often does not fit; in the docs' testing only one or two of five to ten routes did. The executed route can therefore be worse than the best quote, and the example code does not retry or fall back when no route fits. (medium confidence)

Kamino's docs say the amount of LSTs deposited across Solana DeFi far outweighs the liquidity in DEX pools, so moderate selling can cause a temporary market depeg; they name large DEX sell orders and Solana's roughly 2-day epoch unstaking delay as causes of dislocation. Inference: exit capacity for SOL LST loops is DEX depth plus whatever instant-unstake liquidity exists (for example the Sanctum Infinity reserve), not the headline supply of the LST. (medium confidence)

Published negative-carry tests compare the Aave borrow APY with the sUSDe reward yield only, so they leave out incentives that may keep loops open. Sentora's watch metric is 'Aave borrow APY minus sUSDe yield staying < 0'. CryptoSlate calls the loop negative 'before incentives, transaction costs, and other frictions'. Chaos Labs says loopers amplify 'sUSDe rewards and Ethena points', and that the liquid-leverage campaign (50% USDe, 50% sUSDe) gives 'a blended return that ultimately matches the sUSDe reward yield across their entire position', which applies Y to collateral that does not earn it unaided. None of the three quantifies the points, so whether a negative-carry loop stays open depends on a term these sources do not measure. (medium confidence)

Multiply opens, adjusts and closes a leveraged position in one atomic transaction built on a klend flash loan (0.001% fee on each open, adjust or close). The docs list the open sequence as flash-borrow, swap through Kamino Swap, deposit collateral, borrow the debt asset, repay the flash loan. The SDK builds two variants: flash-borrow the collateral token (deposit and borrow, which carries the elevation-group request, then swap debt to collateral, then repay) or flash-borrow the debt token (swap first, then deposit and borrow). If any step fails, the whole transaction reverts. (high confidence)

Interest accrual moves the liquidation price while the position is open. Kamino's example is a $7,000 USDC debt at a 10% borrow rate with flat prices, which drifts from 70% LTV to 77% over 12 months. For a LST/SOL loop the drift equals borrow cost minus staking yield on the leveraged balance: it is upward only when the spread is negative. A static liquidation price quoted at entry is therefore stale after entry. (medium confidence)

Galaxy's implied-loops heuristic is N = ln((1 - (D/E)*(1 - L))/L) / ln(L), with L the debt-weighted average LTV and D/E the debt-weighted average debt/equity, taken on loans where one symbol is at least 99% of collateral. Galaxy calls it a 'sanity-scale' that assumes one asset looped at constant LTV and ignores multi-asset books and execution frictions. (low confidence)

Observed leverage stays below the ceiling for directional loops and runs higher for correlated pairs. IFCA reports most users keep leverage well below the protocol maximum, with leverage capped around 5x for strategies that amplify token price exposure (USD to non-USD assets) because of lower liquidation thresholds, and higher for correlated pairs such as ETH to ETH LSTs and yield-bearing stablecoin loops. Spark likewise says users rarely exceed 3x to 4x in practice. (medium confidence)

Kamino borrow rates are variable and set by pool utilization, so a positive spread can flip negative during high-utilization periods with no action by the position holder. Kamino's worked example of a negative spread is 3x leverage, 6% collateral yield and 8% borrow rate. (medium confidence)

High-LTV eMode positions have a thin buffer against a depeg that is priced into collateral. Kamino's example: a 5% depeg leaves a buffer on a 75% LTV position but may immediately breach the liquidation threshold on a 95% LTV eMode position. Kamino also says a small adverse move in borrow rates has a proportionally larger effect on position health at high leverage. (medium confidence)

Solana's epoch-based native unstaking takes about 2 days (Sanctum says 2-3 days), which limits how fast arbitrage can close an LST discount. Sanctum also says the network caps deactivation at 25% of total staked SOL per epoch, so a mass exit can take longer. (medium confidence)

Stake-pool rate oracles are not dependency-free. Kamino reads the rate directly from each LST's on-chain stake pool account with no off-chain dependency or oracle delay. Jupiter Lend reads the same kind of rate but rejects it if the pool has not been updated in the current epoch or if a deposit or withdrawal fee exceeds 0.5%, and it limits market-feed age to 10 minutes for user operations and 2 hours for liquidations. Before relying on a venue in a stress, check what it does when the rate is rejected or stale. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Fixed-rate borrowing turns B into a known input for the term, at a price. Kamino says fixed-rate borrowing 'allows locking the borrow cost for the full term of a position, converting a variable-spread strategy into a predictable one', at the cost of 'typically paying a small premium over the variable rate at time of entry'. Notional charges an upfront fee on entry and on exit before maturity, and warns that its fixed borrow maturities 'may not align exactly with PT expirations': when fixed debt matures it 'converts to a variable rate', which reintroduces rate risk until the PT expires. (medium confidence)

The execution route changes both the realised entry leverage and the cost. Kamino's developer docs say manual looping takes '8-10 separate transactions', is 'Exposed to price changes between each step' and takes 'Slippage on each swap individually'. They add that if borrow rates spike mid-loop 'you may end up with a worse position than intended — or fail to complete the loop entirely'. Atomic Multiply uses one flash-loan transaction with a 'single consolidated slippage check' and a 0.001% flash-loan fee, charged on open, adjust and close. The SENTRA Fluid example models six swaps in and six out. A quoted Net APY assumes the target L and the quoted B hold at entry; the same Kamino table lists no price exposure between steps for the atomic route and exposure at each step for the manual route. (medium confidence)

Kamino documents the net APY equation as (Collateral Yield x Leverage) - (Borrow Rate x (Leverage - 1)), states that a negative spread has no floor, and warns that borrow rates are variable by utilization, so a positive spread can flip negative with no action by the holder. Kamino's strategies page names sustained SOL borrow rates above LST staking yield as the primary risk for SOL LST Multiply. (high confidence)

Loopscale and Kamino both offer fixed-rate borrowing for loops. Loopscale's loops use fixed-rate loans and earn only while the LST yield exceeds the fixed rate. Kamino's docs say a fixed rate removes borrow-rate risk but typically costs a small premium over the variable rate at entry. No current fixed SOL borrow rate was found for either venue, so fixed-rate carry cannot be quantified from the sources read. (medium confidence)

Kamino-run auto-deleverage is a last-resort tool initiated by its Risk Council under extreme systemic stress: positions get a 72-hour warning, it targets the largest leveraged positions, and Kamino says it has never been triggered. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Kamino applies a borrow factor to debt: borrow capacity = collateral value x Max LTV / borrow factor. A factor of 2.0 doubles the effective risk-adjusted LTV for the same real debt, so a position can be closer to liquidation than the raw market-value LTV suggests. A liquidation price computed from raw values needs the borrow factor applied to debt. (low confidence)

Reserve caps and available liquidity bound how much looping a market can absorb, whatever its LTV. Aave's supply and borrow caps 'limit the total amount of a token that can be supplied and borrowed from a reserve'. Kamino curators can set a borrow limit per collateral inside each elevation group and a separate limit outside groups. Baude et al. add the liquidity constraint x*(l - 1) <= S - B (a loop cannot borrow more than the pool holds) and note that rates explode near full utilization, so it rarely binds. (medium confidence)

Kamino states the Jito Market (SOL) has an interest-rate cap mechanism that bounds rate spikes for JitoSOL/SOL strategies. Kamino describes this as a deliberate limit on the primary risk of its highest-leverage LST product. This is a single vendor claim and the cap parameters were not verified. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

An LST/SOL loop has two separate failure modes. A depeg is a price event: the LST trades below its stake-pool value. A rate inversion is a carry event: the SOL borrow rate rises above the LST yield. Kamino's Multiply docs rate depeg risk 'Eliminated (stake oracle)' and borrow-rate risk 'Primary risk' for SOL LST strategies. Galaxy's July 2025 analysis of ETH loops shows the two modes feed each other: a borrow-rate spike forced unwinds, and the unwinds deepened the LST discount. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

When the rate curve cannot restore liquidity (market-wide stress when borrowers cannot repay, or deliberate utilization attacks), Kamino relies on daily caps, supply caps and auto-deleverage. Its Risk Council can unwind the largest leveraged positions after a 72-hour warning to protect solvency; Kamino says this has never been used. A looper should treat that as a forced-exit risk that is independent of the position's own health. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

If the flash loan cannot be repaid (slippage beyond tolerance, insufficient liquidity, or any other failure), the whole Kamino Multiply transaction reverts and no state changes. A slippage tolerance that is too tight for the unwind size therefore shows up as a failed close, not as a partial fill. (medium confidence)

On the Kamino Swap page, price impact is computed before execution and shown with a warning at 1% or more and an error at 5% or more. Max slippage is a revert cap (the worked example uses 50 bps), the Swap product adds no platform fee, and it queries 15+ routing engines concurrently, with Jupiter/Metis, DFlow and OKX handling most volume. The page states no default tolerance and does not say whether Multiply closes apply the same warning thresholds. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Inference from Kamino's docs: an atomic unwind needs idle cash in the reserves it touches. Kamino lists insufficient liquidity as a cause of flash loan revert, and its risk page says that at 100% utilization lenders cannot withdraw until borrowers repay or new supply arrives. A deleverage that needs more of the debt token or collateral than the reserve holds idle fails as a whole, or must be staged in smaller steps. (medium confidence)

Manual unwinding is the antipattern the flash-loan routes replace. Kamino's comparison (written for building loops) says manual looping takes 8-10 transactions, exposes the user to price moves between steps and slippage on every swap, while atomic Multiply has a single consolidated slippage check. The academic paper models stETH deleveraging as a repeated swap-repay-withdraw cycle on Curve, and BGD notes that health-factor limits can make a one-shot swap impossible without a flash loan. (medium confidence)

Flash-loan deleveraging on Kamino is SDK-only. The docs say the Multiply helpers (getDepositWithLeverageIxs, getWithdrawWithLeverageIxs, getRepayWithCollIxs) exist only in the TypeScript SDK, the REST API cannot build flash loans, and the Rust klend-interface crate exposes flash-loan primitives but not the combo helpers. The examples pin @kamino-finance/kswap-sdk 2.9.0 with klend-sdk 13. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Kamino can force a deleveraging. Its Risk Council may start auto-deleveraging, a systematic reduction of the largest leveraged positions, after a 72-hour warning to the affected positions; Kamino says it has never been triggered. The risk page lists auto-deleverage as the last step of its escalation path. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

A Kamino Multiply unwind runs as one atomic transaction around a klend flash loan: flash-borrow one token, repay the debt, withdraw the freed collateral, swap collateral to the debt token through KSwap, repay the flash loan, and pay the remainder to the wallet (the order of swap and repay depends on the flash shape, see the next claim). If the swap or any other step leaves the flash repay short, the whole transaction reverts and no state changes. The klend program enforces the pairing on-chain by reading the transaction's instruction list: a flash borrow must be followed in the same transaction by exactly one matching flash repay (same amount, same accounts, correct borrow-instruction index), a second flash borrow in the transaction is rejected with 'Multiple flash borrows not allowed', a missing repay fails with 'No flash repay found', and neither instruction may be called through CPI. A wrapper program therefore cannot hold a Kamino flash loan open on its own, and one flash-loan unwind cannot span transactions (a larger unwind has to be several separate flash-loan transactions). (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-19)

A flash-loan unwind needs idle cash in the flash-borrowed reserve, and the SDK refuses to build the transaction when neither reserve has it. determineFlashBorrowType requires flash loans to be enabled on the reserve and enough available liquidity: for coll-flash the collateral reserve must cover the flash borrow plus the collateral redeemed in the same transaction, for debt-flash the debt reserve must cover the whole repay amount. The code comments that a thin collateral reserve can satisfy the flash borrow alone yet still revert with InsufficientLiquidity (klend error 6008) once the redeem is added on top, and that debt-flash is the safe choice for thin or nascent LST reserves on withdraw or close. If neither side qualifies it throws 'Neither collateral nor debt reserve supports flash borrowing the required amount'. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20)

Kamino values SOL LST collateral at the stake-pool exchange rate, not the DEX price, so a market depeg changes neither LTV nor liquidation status. Its docs state the assumptions behind that: LST deposits across Solana DeFi far outweigh DEX liquidity, arbitrageurs are expected to buy a discounted LST and unstake it, and if arbitrage fails (for example a stake pool bug that blocks unstaking) the protocol could hold collateral valued above what the market will pay, with any bad debt socialized among lenders in the affected market. The Multiply risk table lists SOL LST depeg risk as 'Eliminated (stake oracle)' and borrow-rate risk as the primary risk. (medium confidence)

Higher eMode LTVs shrink the gap between operating LTV and the liquidation threshold, so at near-max leverage a modest adverse move in the yield spread (staking yield minus SOL borrow rate) matters more. Kamino names sustained borrow rate above LST yield, and LST smart-contract exploits, as the main liquidation paths for SOL-LST Multiply rather than SOL price moves. (medium confidence)

Kamino publishes a checklist rather than a formula. Before enabling a group, curators should confirm member correlation (test depeg and divergence history), pick the single most liquid or most wanted debt_reserve, cap max_reserves_as_collateral, tighten max_liquidation_bonus_bps to realistic correlated-asset slippage, set per-collateral group borrow limits, and set disable_usage_as_coll_outside_emode to 1 for LSTs (often 0 for stables). Reference ranges are 88-92% LTV and 90-95% threshold for LSTs against their underlying, and 90-95% and 92-97% for stables-only groups. (medium confidence)

For SOL-denominated LST loops (JitoSOL, mSOL, bSOL, JupSOL against SOL debt) Kamino prices the LST by stake rate, LST price = SOL_staked / LST_minted, not by DEX price. Both sides move with SOL, so LTV does not change with SOL's USD price. The liquidation variable is therefore the exchange rate plus the yield-versus-borrow spread. A market discount, such as JitoSOL at 0.95 SOL, does not raise reported LTV. Stake-rate pricing does not protect against a real loss of staked SOL (exploit, slashing), which lowers the exchange rate itself. (medium confidence)

For LST/SOL loops the liquidation variable is the LST exchange rate plus the borrow-versus-yield spread, not SOL's dollar price. Kamino prices LSTs at the stake rate, LST price = SOL_staked / LST_minted, which rises each epoch, so a DEX discount (its example: JitoSOL at 0.95 SOL) does not change LTV. Jupiter Lend pegged vaults price on an on-chain exchange or redemption rate, and its docs add that a drop in that rate (slashing, or a loss in the underlying strategy) can also bring a position to liquidation. Both vendors say stake-rate pricing removes market-noise liquidations but not a real loss of backing. The on-chain oracle configuration of these reserves was not verified in this pass. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

A flash loan builds the position in one transaction instead of n rounds. Borrow F = k*c0 (k = extra multiple of initial collateral c0), swap into collateral, deposit, borrow against the total, repay the flash loan. The borrow constraint B/C = k/(k+1) <= L gives k <= L/(1-L), so total collateral is at most c0/(1-L), the same ceiling as the infinite loop. (medium confidence)

Health-factor buffer depends on the collateral mix. In 1inch's July 2026 Aave case study, a book at HF 1.18 had a 48.8% price buffer because stablecoin collateral absorbed debt, versus about 15.3% for a pure-WETH book at the same HF. A collateral transfer then cut the buffer from 34.2% to 0.2% and the wallet was liquidated. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-22)

Kamino Multiply, Jupiter Lend Multiply and the Cyfrin flash-leverage lesson describe the same atomic build: flash-borrow the debt asset, swap it into the collateral asset, deposit the user's funds plus the swapped collateral, borrow the debt asset against that deposit, and repay the flash loan from the borrow. All steps run in one transaction, so if any step fails (slippage, liquidity) nothing is committed. Jupiter says Multiply 'reaches the target leverage in one pass rather than by repeating loops'. (high confidence)

Kamino and Jupiter Lend both value LSTs at the stake-pool exchange rate rather than the DEX price. Kamino computes LST price = SOL_staked / LST_minted from the on-chain stake pool account. Jupiter Lend reads the stake pool's accounting rate for JupSOL, JitoSOL and mSOL. A temporary DEX discount therefore does not move LTV or trigger liquidation on these venues. (high confidence)

Kamino and Jupiter Lend both value LSTs at the stake-pool exchange rate, not the DEX price. Kamino computes LST price = SOL_staked / LST_minted and reads it from each LST's on-chain stake pool account, with no off-chain dependency. Jupiter Lend uses the SPL stake pool accounting rate for JupSOL, JitoSOL and similar tokens, and Marinade's accounting rate for mSOL. A temporary DEX discount therefore leaves LTV unchanged and triggers no liquidation on these venues. Jupiter adds that these rates 'can differ from the amount you would receive by selling or redeeming the token'. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Stake-rate pricing removes market-noise liquidations but not fundamental loss, and it assumes arbitrage will close the gap: buyers purchase the discounted LST, unstake it for SOL at the stake rate and keep the difference. If a staking-pool issue blocks unstaking and a depeg persists, the lending protocol can hold collateral valued above what the market will pay. Kamino says that scenario risks bad debt, with losses socialized among lenders of the affected market, and lists supply caps, per-LST risk review and stake-pool monitoring as mitigations. Jupiter Lend likewise warns that its contract-based rates can differ from what selling or redeeming the token would return. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Monitor the spread, not the headline APY. Kamino says to watch the yield spread continuously rather than the APY shown when a position opened, and its Liquidation Analysis Suite simulates time-to-liquidation under borrow-rate scenarios, finds break-even leverage and yield, and backtests past market events. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The formula rearranges to Net = Y + (Y−B)×(L−1): unlevered yield plus the yield spread earned on each borrowed dollar. Kamino writes it as 'Net APY = Collateral Yield + Yield Spread × (Leverage − 1)'. SODAX writes it as effectiveNet = effectiveSupply + leverage × spread, where its 'leverage' is the borrowed amount per unit of deposit (that is, L−1), so the two forms are algebraically identical. Check which convention a calculator uses before comparing numbers. (high confidence)

Yield-side inputs in calculators may be trailing averages. SODAX takes the LSD staking yield from DefiLlama's latest apy value (a trailing 7-30 day window, per the SODAX doc) and falls back to a hardcoded value flagged stale:true if the fetch fails, so a calculator's Y can lag the live rate. (low confidence)

The formula rearranges to Net = Y + (L−1)×(Y−B): the unlevered yield plus the spread earned on each borrowed unit. Kamino writes 'Collateral Yield + Yield Spread × (Leverage − 1)'; CryptoTicker writes 'result = yield + borrowed units × (yield − borrow rate)'. SODAX writes effectiveNet = effectiveSupply + leverage × spread, but its 'leverage' is debt ÷ equity = targetLTV/(1−targetLTV) = L−1; its code comment says this is 'Not total exposure' and that a UI 'Leverage' label shows 1 + that value. Check whether a calculator's 'leverage' means L or L−1 before comparing numbers. (high confidence)

Calculator outputs differ in ways that change the answer. Kamino's open-position screen shows a Net APY indicator plus a simulation 'based on 180-day historical data' (backward-looking; the docs do not say whether Net APY itself uses spot or trailing rates). SODAX's SDK exposes two numbers: getApr() uses lending-pool rates only and can read negative, while getEffectiveApr() adds the LSD staking yield. Jupiter Lend's Liquidation Calculator estimates how long a position takes to reach liquidation under chosen borrow-rate scenarios. (medium confidence)

Kamino's Multiply interface has a Liquidation Analysis Suite that lets a user 'adjust leverage and theoretical yield to see break-even thresholds', simulate time-to-liquidation under different borrow-rate scenarios, and run historical backtests. The docs advise using it before opening any leveraged position, particularly for JLP and xStocks. They do not say whether its break-even uses the spot or a trailing B. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Jupiter Lend also documents borrow rates as variable, adjusting with the utilization of each asset, and a Loopscale doc describes its JupSOL/SOL loop as earning only while the JupSOL staking APY exceeds Loopscale's fixed borrow rate. Variable-rate venues expose the loop to rate swings; the fixed-rate venue exposes it to a locked rate set at entry. (medium confidence)

Kamino prices SOL LSTs by stake rate (SOL staked / LST minted), read from the stake pool account, not by DEX price. A market discount, such as JitoSOL at 0.95 SOL against a 1.05 SOL stake rate, does not change a Multiply position's LTV. A real loss of backing (exploit, slashing) lowers the stake rate and does change it. Kamino says this is why market depegs have not liquidated LST Multiply positions. (medium confidence)

Aave defines Health Factor = (Total Collateral Value x Weighted Average Liquidation Threshold) / Total Borrow Value; HF below 1 permits liquidation. The liquidation threshold is set per collateral asset by Aave governance. For a single collateral asset whose debt price is fixed, setting HF = 1 and solving gives liquidation price = debt / (collateral amount x liquidation threshold); this rearrangement is derived here, not quoted from Aave. The same bound can be written as a tolerable price drop of 1 - 1/HF. (high confidence)

Bank of Canada Staff Analytical Paper 2026-13 (Chiu and Danisman, April 2026) studies Aave V3 and finds many users engage in recursive leverage despite overcollateralization requirements, and that liquidations occur in concentrated waves. The abstract page gives no prevalence percentage. (low confidence)

Max-borrow LTV and liquidation threshold are separate, governance-set parameters that vary by market and change over time. Aave defines LTV as 'the maximum amount that can be borrowed relative to the collateral's value' and the liquidation threshold as 'the collateral ratio at which a position can be liquidated' (health factor below 1). Kamino elevation groups carry ltv_pct and liquidation_threshold_pct, which must be >= ltv_pct. Jupiter Lend says positions must stay under the vault's maximum LTV, 'which is below the Liquidation Threshold'. (high confidence)

Three published rules count looping on-chain, and they measure different things. The Bank of Canada flags a borrow of B against A, followed within one day by a swap of B back into A, followed within the next day by a new borrow against that A (an approximation; longer windows gave no significant difference). IFCA rebuilds each address's collateral and debt from deposit, withdraw, borrow and repay flows and computes leverage = C*Pc/(C*Pc - D*Pd). Galaxy uses balance-sheet snapshots: debt-weighted LTV and debt/equity per collateral asset, inverted into an implied loop count. Results from the three are not directly comparable. (medium confidence)

In a Kamino Multiply LST loop, Net APY = Collateral Yield + Yield Spread x (Leverage - 1), where Yield Spread = collateral yield minus borrow rate. A negative spread grows more negative with leverage, and Kamino states there is no floor. (medium confidence)

Stress tests in the same study found that leverage staking amplifies cascading liquidations under a severe stETH devaluation. Liquidations and the leveraged users' own deleveraging add selling pressure on stETH, which deepens the devaluation and spreads liquidation to ordinary (non-leveraged) positions. Kamino's LST-oracle page describes the same loop for market-price oracles. (medium confidence)

Whether a market depeg liquidates a loop depends on the venue's oracle. Kamino prices Solana LSTs at the stake rate (SOL_staked / LST_minted), read from the on-chain stake pool account, so its docs say a JitoSOL DEX price of 0.95 SOL leaves positions valued at about 1.02 SOL unaffected. Jupiter Lend also prices JupSOL, JitoSOL and similar tokens by the SPL stake-pool accounting rate (mSOL by Marinade's rate, INF by the Infinity pool rate) and states that these rates 'are not market prices'. Kamino describes a market-price oracle as the cascade-prone alternative: every brief LST depeg would liquidate healthy positions, and the forced sales would deepen the depeg. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
